items.text: Sanskrit: the first pulse. The vibration that precedes understanding.
Paw-shaped. Handheld. Held against the chest. When you hold it, you receive the animal’s state as a sensation.
To receive another’s presence, you must first choose to be present. Deliberate, conscious.

The Problem Solving module asks you to frame your own problem and write your own brief. That means working through ambiguity and vagueness before there is a problem at all.
I started wide, with every place communication happens without words, and followed the branch about animals and humans.
Cross-species · young children · differently abled · shock and trauma · high stakes · power display · intimacy · digital · environmental

items.text: Three contexts came out of it: the street, the home and the zoo. For each, I put together a context sheet, wrote scenarios (setting, persona, trigger, action, internal state, friction) and How Might We questions, then clustered and voted on them.
Ahmedabad has about 1.5 lakh street dogs by current AMC estimates. Anti-rabies vaccinations have surged to 7,500 a month. The AMC has notified only 126 designated feeding spots for the entire city.
Vibes of India, Jan 2026; Times of India, Jan 2026.

A commuter walking to their scooter unknowingly crosses a “Safe Zone” boundary, marked by scent and historical use. The dog gives a low warning growl; the human, blind to the boundary, keeps walking. The human thinks they are on a public sidewalk. The dog thinks they are an intruder breaching a private residence.
Other scenarios: The Silent “No” · The Anonymous Nuisance · The “Night-Biker” Chase · The Survival Silhouette
The HMWs clustered into territorial maps, predatory triggers and sensory understanding, and narrowed to three:

the where
How might we help a commuter navigate and respect the invisible territorial boundaries of street dogs?

the how
How might we bridge the sensory gap between human motion and a dog’s predatory triggers to de-escalate the urban ‘menace’ narrative?

the who
How might we dismantle the ‘stray menace’ label by surfacing the individual history and character of neighborhood dogs, shifting their status from ‘nuisance’ to ‘resident subject’?

items.text: India’s pet dog population is projected to hit 43.9 million by late 2026, with 63% of urban households owning at least one dog. Ahmedabad sees only a 38% registration rate. 70% of the city’s new pet owners live in high-rises, where the service lift is the primary interface.

An owner discovers a chewed remote and scolds the dog with a towering posture and angry tone. The dog lowers its head, shows “whale eyes” and avoids eye contact. The owner says, “See? He knows he’s guilty.” The “Guilty Look” is a survival mechanism to de-escalate human anger.
Other scenarios: The Elevator Breach · The Acoustic Smog · The Rest Violation · The Resource War · Unpreparedness
The HMWs clustered into sensory experiences and stress signals, behavioural boundaries and autonomy, and realistic pet needs, and narrowed to one:
How might we make a pet’s invisible sensory load perceptible to humans so that biological stress is no longer mistranslated as ‘bad behavior’?

items.text: Sunday, 11:30 AM, at the tiger enclosure. A father and a 6-year-old stand at the railing. The tiger is sitting 25 feet away across the moat, staring at the horizon. The child asks, “Papa, is it real or a toy?” because it hasn’t moved for three minutes. The father whistles loudly and waves his arms. The 20-foot gap makes the tiger feel like a 3D movie or a statue.

Other scenarios: The “Invisible” Predator · The “Clown” in the Cage · The Observation Wall · It’s just a Lion. For keepers: The “Snapshot” Audit · The Memory Tax. For the animals: The “Static” Enrichment Loop · The “Privacy” Vacuum.

The HMWs clustered into animal observation and behaviour interpretation, animal welfare and autonomy, physical and spatial design, and data capture and monitoring. The zoo HMW became the design question below.

items.text: Why zoo? The clearest place to design: highest density of encounters, most visible breakdown, and a live policy mandate to fix it.

Zoo visits are mostly about recognising and identifying animals, and not relating to them. This creates a distance where visitors disengage, provoke animals to trigger a reaction, and treat them as objects of spectacle.

children.text: The moment they see a new animal, then moving on.
Through anthropomorphic labels: “it’s happy,” “it’s bored,” “it’s being lazy.”
To elicit a response, and when nothing comes, apathy.
ambient noise, with a documented correlation with increased cortisol and pacing in leopards (ResearchGate 2025)
provocation rate in high-density viewing zones, a global baseline (MDPI Animals 2023)

items.text: About 5,500 visitors on a weekday. Entry is ₹20 for adults and ₹10 for children, which positions it as a cheap “outing” more than an educational visit.
The 43rd CZA meeting (3 Feb 2026) mandated that zoos transition from “display centres” to spaces for “research, learning, and inspiring empathy.”
The 44th CZA meeting (28 Feb 2026) instructed schools to hold “exclusive classes” to seek “collective suggestions for strengthening zoos” following visits.
MoS Shri Kirti Vardhan Singh called for technology and stakeholder collaboration to improve zoos from the “viewer’s perspective”, to counter the “loss of sensitivity” in younger generations.

School-aged children. 6 to 14. Organised group visits. Highest provocation rate of any visitor group. Lowest biodiversity literacy. First and often only direct encounter with these animals. What lands here lands for life.
Primary research at Indroda Nature Park and Kankaria Zoo, Ahmedabad.

children.text: Nobody read a signboard, including me.
The animal wasn’t doing anything, so visitors tried to make it do something.
The leopard responded differently to different people.
Calm observers got calm behaviour. Loud visitors got charges.
He had known the leopard since it was a cub. The leopard snuggled with him.
A one-horned deer kept moving its head up and down.
I wanted to know why. There was no way to find out.

items.text: The animal was reading the room. Nobody in the room knew that.
The gap is the ability to receive what the animal is already broadcasting.
The zoo’s How Might We questions clustered into three groups. Each group named a different kind of illiteracy.

children.text: I don’t know who you are as an individual.
I can’t read what your body is saying.
I cannot perceive the frequency you exist in.

items.text: Signs, guides, and plaques address biographical illiteracy at best. Behavioural and sensorial remain mostly unattended to.

children.text: Zoo visitors’ score on biodiversity literacy. They consistently misread stress responses as entertainment.

items.text: Leopards operate in infrasound and spatial acoustic maps imperceptible to humans. The gap is hardware.
What the tiger is actually doing

children.text: 40–50 BPM resting heart rate. Ears rotating independently, mapping every footfall in the corridor. Vigilant acoustic mapping.
Infrasound reception: processing territorial signals below 20Hz, completely inaudible to humans. It is listening to a frequency we cannot hear.
Stereotypic pacing, zoochosis. Repetitive locomotion from spatial frustration. A coping mechanism. The zoo’s own failure, made physical.
Pinna directionality: involuntary rotation to locate and triangulate a threat source. The ear moved because a child shouted three enclosures away.
Flehmen response: drawing scent into the Jacobson’s organ to read the reproductive and social status of every animal and human in the space.

items.text: Typical visitor remarks, and the tiger’s umwelt behind them.
How some traditions relate to animals
This knowledge existed. We designed it out. Indigenous and traditional communities did not have this gap.
Humans and animals depicted at equal scale, in shared ecological space. Cohabitation.
Western Ghats leopard and tiger deity. The animal is a presence to be respected. Territorial boundaries acknowledged before approach.
A cross-cultural practice of temporarily inhabiting an animal’s body schema to understand its state. Embodied empathy as a method.

items.text: The chest contains CT afferents that route to the interoceptive cortex. The body reads the signal as coming from within. The wrist is informational touch. The chest is affective touch.

items.text: Translucent tinted polycarbonate, satin finish. Electronics visible inside.
Soft-touch silicone rubber. 5 contact points, 5 actuators.
Braided nylon. Secure handling in high-density environments.

DA7280 LRA: central pad, heartbeat + resonance.
4× ERM: toe pads, directional rhythm.
NeoPixel strip: edge, valence layer.
ESP32-C3: wireless control.
Neo6M GPS: locator.
TTP223: touch sensor for activation.
Translucent by design. The child sees it working. Transparency as consent.

items.text: Most educational media routes through the brain first; signs, screens, audio guides land in the cognitive layer, the same layer where we project narratives onto what we see. Haptics bypass that layer entirely.

Two approaches. Where a biological rhythm exists, such as a heartbeat or a breath, we mirror it directly. Where it doesn’t, we use rhythm rate and envelope shape as the emotional lever. Slow and smooth reads as calm. Fast and jagged reads as threat. The body already knows this.
Rhythm is the single parameter that independently modulates valence, arousal, and perceived roughness. Only naturalistic, biomimetic patterns reliably reach calm-pleasant states in children.
Every pattern decision was checked against research on affective haptics.

children.text: Rhythm rate shapes emotional valence far more than the carrier frequency. (Azevedo et al., 2017; Costa et al., 2016)
Calm states are reached with naturalistic rhythms like breath and heartbeat. Abstract codes fail, especially with children. (Shim & Tan, 2020)
No standard mapping between vibration patterns and emotions exists yet.

items.text: I scored candidate behaviours on Frequency (how often it happens), Gap (how invisible or misread it is to visitors) and Viability (whether it can be sensed and felt). An early map suggested a purr for contentment; tigers and leopards don’t purr, so it went.

items.text: The child calibrates at entry, during a brief onboarding, to felt metaphors. Intensity set, mystery intact.
At the enclosure, GPS confirms which animal they are standing in front of. In multi-animal enclosures, one hero individual is foregrounded via signage.
The trigger is either a keeper who knows the animal’s current state, or the CV pipeline reading it live. Either way, what arrives in the child’s chest is presence.

items.text: SPANDA is trained on individuals. Keepers log daily behavioural observations per named animal. That data builds the model.
The hero animal selected for each enclosure is the one the child will feel: ‘Prathap’, one named leopard. This is what makes attribution possible, and attribution is what makes empathy possible.
A newer training pipeline: coming soon.

Why this works
Why this should work, hopefully*

children.text: Chest CT afferents read the signal as internal. (McGlone et al., 2014; Löken et al., 2009)
Rhythm is the primary emotional lever. (Seifi & MacLean, 2013)
Biomimetic patterns reach calm states; abstract codes fail. (Shim & Tan, 2020)
The torso yields 99–100% pattern recognition accuracy. (Jones et al., 2009)
Vibration conveys valence without projection. (Ju & Minamizawa, CHI EA 2023)
Haptic wearables increase nature connectedness in zoos. (Chen et al., IJHCI 2025)

items.text: FAQs (frequently asked to me, by me)
Highest provocation rate. Lowest literacy. Longest memory. A felt experience at 8 years old shapes how you see an animal for the rest of your life.
Sound is processed cognitively. We assign meaning, narrative, and emotion to what we hear. Haptics bypass that layer. The body receives before the brain interprets.
What if the animal isn’t visible?
SPANDA defaults to resting heartbeat. Presence felt even when presence is hidden.
One hero individual foregrounded per enclosure, introduced by name via signage. SPANDA is calibrated to that individual.
CV pipeline handles it. Keeper presence enables richer contextual triggering. No keeper means the system runs autonomously. Both are valid.
How do you handle haptic subjectivity?
Metaphor-based calibration at entry sets individual intensity and sensitivity. Long term, each calibration becomes a data point for a learning model.
Keepers already log daily behavioural observations. SPANDA plugs into that existing workflow. Each enclosure gets a trained model per individual animal. The pipeline is repeatable.
The metaphor-based calibration exists as a concept. The kiosk interface, the child-facing flow, the sensitivity logic are all unbuilt. Designing that experience is the next design problem.

Currently a bare web panel for demo triggering. A proper keeper interface would let staff log behavioural observations in real time, flag state changes, and build the ethogram directly through daily interaction with the device. A full design project in itself.
In place of “Indian Leopard, Panthera pardus fusca”: Dharma. 7 years old. Currently resting. Signage that makes the animal a subject.
Each calibration a data point. The system gets better at knowing which patterns land for which bodies. The framework keeps getting learnt.
One that doesn’t exist yet in this project or in the literature. SPANDA is the first attempt to need one.

The CV pipeline currently reads pose and spatial velocity. Next: directional microphones picking up vocalisation, thermal cameras reading body heat and respiration, ground vibration sensors detecting movement through substrate. More of the animal’s inner life translatable, including when it isn’t visible.
